description: How mobile app distribution shifted when Apple tightened control while Android kept growing—measured in global mobile OS share across the defining iPhone era.
unit: Percent share of global smartphone OS
youtube_description:
⏳ From 2009’s early iPhone wave to the App Store era—and then the Android rebound—this chart race shows how mobile OS power shifted as Apple tightened the app funnel while Android kept expanding globally.

CHAPTERS
00:00 — The starting line (2009): iOS climbs, Android dominates
01:20 — 2013–2015: iOS strength peaks in the App Store era
03:10 — 2016–2018: the balance tightens, Android keeps momentum
05:05 — 2019–2020: a sudden iOS dip vs Android’s surge
06:40 — 2021–2025: the new stable era (iOS holds ~27–28%)

What you’ll see in motion:
• iOS rises into the mid-30s, then settles into a steady premium plateau.
• Android stays the mass-market engine—then clearly reasserts during 2020–2025.
• BlackBerry and Windows Phone collapse to near-zero as developers consolidate.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The App Store Tightening vs the Android Machine… in numbers.

In 2009, smartphones were still shaking hands with the future. Android owned the majority share at ~80%, while iOS sat around ~20%. But the iPhone era wasn’t just about hardware—it was about distribution. By 2011, iOS was up near ~27%, riding a wave of App Store adoption and early “premium-first” user behavior.

Then the dramatic middle arrives: 2013–2015. iOS climbs from ~35% to roughly ~43% (while Android slides from ~65% to ~57%). This is the moment the chart race starts to feel unfair—iOS is winning attention, developers, and high-intent users. BlackBerry, meanwhile, is already bleeding out (dropping from ~3% in 2013 to ~1% by 2015). Windows Phone is basically a ghost story after the early-2010s—down to ~1–2%.

But every good rise meets a counter-move. From 2016 through 2018, iOS slips from about ~40% toward ~38–39% while Android rebuilds its grip (~60% to ~62%). And the real punchline? 2020. Android surges (jumping to about ~74%), while iOS drops sharply to the mid‑20s (~26%). That’s not a “small dip”—that’s the kind of pivot where ecosystems feel friction, then re-route global users toward what’s broadly available.

By 2021–2025, the world settles: iOS stabilizes around ~27–28%, and Android levels at ~72–73%. The losers are long gone: BlackBerry and Windows Phone hover near ~0.1% and ~0.05% respectively—mostly legend now.

🎯 What do you think caused the 2020 iOS dip—regulatory pressure, market shifts, or just the faster Android replenishment cycle?

facebook_caption:
Mobile OS share is the simplest scoreboard for a complex battle: Apple’s App Store-led ecosystem vs. Android’s global distribution machine.

From 2009 to 2015, iOS rose from ~20% to ~43%, peaking in the mid‑30s during 2013–2015 as the App Store era drew users and developers into Apple’s walled-garden model. Android remained the dominant platform, but its share steadily eased from ~80% down to ~57% by 2015.

The turning point came in the late 2010s and accelerated around 2020. iOS eased back from ~40% (2016) to ~37–39% (2017–2019), while Android regained ground, reaching ~74% in 2020 versus iOS at ~26%. After that shock, the market stabilized: iOS held roughly ~27–28% through 2021–2025, while Android remained steady around ~72–73%.

The chart also captures the collapse of challengers. BlackBerry falls toward near-zero (from ~3% in 2013 to ~0.1% by 2024–2025). Windows Phone similarly fades from ~1–2% in the early-mid 2010s to ~0.05% by 2024–2025.

Question: Do you think platform share follows regulation and policy—or mainly consumer replacement cycles?

threads_caption:
Crazy how fast the “smartphone OS” map flipped. 📱

In 2009, iOS was ~20% and Android was ~80%. Then iOS surged hard—mid‑30s by 2013 and ~43% in 2015—while BlackBerry and Windows Phone started collapsing.

But the real plot twist? 2020. Android jumped to about ~74% while iOS fell to ~26%. After that, things calmed down: iOS basically settled around ~27–28%, and Android around ~72–73%.

Would you rather invest in the “ecosystem winner” (apps + retention) or the “distribution winner” (reach + device breadth)?
